title: The invention of equality
gist: David Wootton reviews Teresa Bejan's 'First Among Equals', which argues modern egalitarianism was invented by Leveller John Lilburne in 1646 as a rupture with earlier ancient and Christian ideas of equality that accepted hierarchy. Wootton praises the book as exceptional but faults its cloistered scholarship and its charge that Lilburne and the Quakers were inconsistent egalitarians.

insights.claim: Teresa Bejan argues that modern egalitarianism was invented by John Lilburne in the summer of 1646 in 'The Free-Mans Freedome Vindicated', which held every man and woman to be naturally equal in power and authority, with authority arising only from consent.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Locates the intellectual origin of consent-based legitimacy underlying modern democratic politics.

insights.claim: Bejan contends that equality in Athenian democracy, Stoicism, Roman law and early Christianity was consistent with accepting political, legal, social and economic inequality, so reading those traditions as egalitarian is a misreading.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Challenges the long-lineage narrative of equality.
insights.quote: Their arguments for equality were never egalitarian; when we imagine they were we misread them.

insights.claim: A consequence of Bejan's argument is that Hobbes' Leviathan should be read as a post-Lilburne egalitarian text while his pre-1646 works were non-egalitarian, which Wootton thinks is sustainable though delicate.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Re-dating intellectual shifts changes how foundational political texts are interpreted.

insights.claim: Bejan's account contrasts with Quentin Skinner's 'Liberty Before Liberalism', presenting a single moment of rupture rather than a long evolution towards modernity, and rejecting Locke as the paradigmatic modern theorist because he allowed deference within civil society.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Frames competing historiographies of liberal political thought.
insights.locator: Teresa Bejan has answers to these questions

insights.claim: Bejan holds that equality is foundational only because people have come to believe it is (a 'Tinkerbell Effect'), becoming self-evident only when grounded in egalitarian practice such as Lilburne's refusal to doff his hat.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Suggests social norms, not arguments, sustain political legitimacy, and can erode if practices change.
insights.locator: Bejan does not find Lilburne’s arguments

insights.claim: Quaker merchants' introduction of a fixed price for every buyer was, as Bejan explains, revolutionary as an egalitarian commercial practice.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Origin story of fixed, non-negotiated retail pricing as an egalitarian market innovation.
insights.locator: Bejan is surprisingly keen to accuse

insights.claim: Wootton argues Bejan wrongly convicts Quakers of failing to assert slaves' equality, citing the 1688 Germantown Quakers asking whether enslaved people had as much right to fight for their freedom as slaveholders had to keep them.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Highlights early abolitionist reasoning in commercial religious communities.
insights.locator: Bejan is surprisingly keen to accuse

insights.claim: Wootton contends Bejan misreads Lilburne's 1649 position: Lilburne argued royalist commanders should be tried by a jury of their neighbours, not by peers in the House of Lords, which is consistent egalitarianism.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Points to the jury-of-equals principle as a core egalitarian legal safeguard.
insights.locator: This leads us to the one point

insights.claim: Wootton finds the book cloistered, with footnotes resembling a political theory reading list, omitting scholars such as Thomson, Seaford, Ashcraft and Ginzburg.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Reviewer quality check on an influential new work in political theory.

insights.claim: Wootton suggests egalitarianism predates 1646 in some form, citing a 1604 taxation pamphlet, 'The Order of Equalitie', as the first to call 'do unto others' the Golden Rule.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Links early egalitarian ideas to debates over fair taxation.
insights.quote: a striking case of egalitarianism before 1646

insights.claim: Wootton says Bejan's work vindicates the Levellers against Mark Kishlansky's 1979 argument that they mattered little at Putney, since Lilburne first insisted equality is the only self-evident foundation for legitimacy.
insights.speaker: David Wootton
insights.so_what: Reassesses the historical importance of radical movements.
